paragraphs: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday evening waiving the sanctions, restrictions and duties in the Graham Act, according to The Hill. Trump signed that Russia sanctions law in September. NPR reported that the order came two days before a deadline set in the law for its implementation. Trump told Congress the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media that a decision was made in America to "completely disregard" the law, which he said was meant to pressure Russia to end the war. NPR reported that he did not directly criticize Trump. He said blocking the law would encourage Russia to keep killing, and that he hoped Trump would do everything possible to make Putin stop attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The Hill reported that Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan he felt "betrayed."

Reaction in Congress split along unusual lines. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis called the move "beyond irresponsible," Sen. John Cornyn wrote that the late Sen. Lindsey Graham "would be appalled," and Rep. Don Bacon said the president is prolonging the war. Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said the waivers had "nothing to do with our national security." Republican Rep. Thomas Massie backed the waiver, calling the law "stupid" and noting he was among seven Republicans who voted against it. The White House's own explanation beyond the certification was not in the reports.

The waiver follows a deal Trump announced last week for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel to ease energy prices. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Russia struck more than 15 energy sites overnight. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones.

Demonstrations took place across France on Saturday over rising living costs, joined by students, teachers, unions and supporters of the revived "yellow vest" movement. NPR reported that a car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris, where police used tear gas and water cannons on masked groups throwing fireworks and other objects in the Place de la République.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office described a growing number of violent incidents, including assaults on police, looting and damage to public buildings, and reported at least 272 arrests nationwide. In Lyon, where about 20,000 people marched, a fire broke out inside a tourist office. In Marseille, shops and a municipal police station were damaged and some protesters briefly entered the City Hall lobby. Mayor Benoît Payan called that unacceptable but described the damage as limited.

Both NPR and Al Jazeera noted that most protesters were peaceful. Al Jazeera's Natacha Butler said the Paris protest "never really got started" because police moved quickly to isolate demonstrators, and that this is where some trouble began. The Interior Ministry had counted 140 protest actions with 32,800 participants by midday, according to Al Jazeera.

The protests follow weeks of student school blockades since mid-September. NPR reported thousands of arrests and hundreds of injuries in that period, and said Nuñez suspended one type of police stun grenade after a 15-year-old lost a hand. The CGT union called for higher wages and pensions and lower prices.

Al Jazeera's Rosie Birchard described this as a key moment, with budget negotiations underway and a presidential election next year. President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that protest is a constitutional right but must respect people and property.

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney told the Scottish National Party's conference in Aberdeen on Saturday that the campaign for a second independence referendum "has already begun," according to The Guardian. He said the party would run its "most sophisticated campaign in history," called Choose Scotland and backed by "a six-figure war chest."

Swinney argued that the "stars were aligning" for independence. He said a recent joint appearance with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland had upset opponents, and that they could no longer portray the nationalists as separatists. He said independence is "very close" and that the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. The Guardian noted that calling a referendum is not in his power, and that the Westminster government would have to grant a second vote.

Other SNP figures described a path through a hung parliament at Westminster. Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said polling suggests the SNP would hold the balance of power and regain seats. MP Lara Bird said the party could negotiate for another poll with the next UK government, and noted polls putting the SNP at between 40 and 50 MPs. The party now holds eight. An Electoral Calculus poll this week predicted a narrow Labour win with the SNP taking 28 seats, though The Guardian said there is uncertainty over how many it would gain.

UK prime minister Andy Burnham, visiting Lanarkshire on Friday, said the Scottish government needed to "move beyond" the constitutional question and focus on the cost of living. He offered to work more closely with Swinney on devolving power from Holyrood.

Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican, after doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed he was well enough to go home. NPR reported that he walked out without physical support and waved to well-wishers. The discharge came sooner than had been expected when the operation was announced.

Leo, 71, told crowds last Sunday that doctors had found a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage." Tuesday's surgery went further than the nodule: surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung in an operation of about 90 minutes. Doctors said tissue examined afterward confirmed lung adenocarcinoma. The BBC reported that results of further tests to check whether the cancer has spread have not been announced. NPR said the Vatican has announced no further treatment.

Doctors not involved in his care told NPR the signs are encouraging. Dr. Vin Gupta said using surgery first suggests an early-stage cancer, and that removing more lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said estimated recovery time is about one week. Leo is not known to have smoked, NPR reported, though cancer runs in his family. The Vatican said his older brother Louis has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.

The pope is expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the papal apartment window on Sunday. His public schedule is cleared until at least Oct. 20. A trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru is planned for early November, though the BBC said it is not yet clear whether he will be fit to travel.

Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, have asked the Justice Department to return property federal agents took from her home during a search on Monday. In a letter reported by the Associated Press, they called the seizure "neither justified nor lawful." They also demanded that the department preserve any audio and video recorded during the search.

The Guardian reported that the lawyers wrote there is "no legitimate basis" for suggesting she violated any law concerning her citizenship status. They accused the department of breaking its policy aimed at avoiding influence on elections, and raised questions about whether investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search. Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said the letter was "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and that attorneys and law enforcement complied with all court orders.

Fox News reported that the investigation concerns allegations that Omar or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork. The claim is that she was 18, not 17, when her father became a citizen in 2000. Omar has denied related allegations, and The Guardian described earlier claims about her ex-husband as unsubstantiated. Federal authorities have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to relatives, and seized her phone.

Omar called the search an attempt to target political enemies. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other Democrats called it weaponization of the federal government. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, a Minnesota Republican, told Fox that if the allegations are proven she should serve time and be deported, and that a judge's finding of probable cause shows the case is not political. Trump denied involvement, saying the matter has nothing to do with him. The midterm elections are on Nov. 3.

Both the United States and Iran say they control the Strait of Hormuz, even as ships keep being attacked there, Al Jazeera reported. The UK Maritime Trade Operations center said at least 12 ships were attacked in the week ending Oct. 16, but warned that most attacked vessels refuse to report to it, so the true number is hard to pin down. Of the 12 confirmed, half continued or reached port, one sank and two were disabled.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a video message that 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moved through the strait in the past week. He said the strait is controlled by the United States and its regional partners, not Iran, and attributed the attacks to "desperation" by the Revolutionary Guard. The US military also says its naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says ships are hitting mines and that vessels not coordinating with Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority are traveling unsafely. On Saturday it said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude caught fire after striking a mine on an unauthorised route. CENTCOM said it had cleared the strait of mines and that ships are being hit by projectiles. It said the container ship GFS Pride, which sank on Thursday, was hit by a Guard projectile. Tehran has said Washington exaggerates its numbers.

Kpler figures show oil flows through Hormuz at about 68 percent of the pre-war level. Brent crude touched $110 a barrel on Friday, the first time since May. Messages are still passing between the sides through mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, but no breakthrough is expected soon. Al Jazeera said there are concerns the US could escalate after the Nov. 3 midterms, while Iran's acting defence minister said Iranian missiles would determine the war's future.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency session of parliament to authorise him to approve any request from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, Al Jazeera reported. Speaking at a military academy graduation on Saturday, he said Egypt would "carry out any measure to protect" Saudi Arabia in line with the directives of King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. He said the authorisation would apply only if Riyadh asks for help.
El-Sisi said he was not speaking in order to fight or attack anyone, but only for defence.

The call follows a barrage of attacks on Saudi Arabia from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, including strikes on airports and oil facilities. Al Jazeera said an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300, and that attacks have also been reported at Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran airports. Yemen's Saudi-backed government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory.

Last month, after the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and gained significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, el-Sisi met the crown prince in Cairo. The Egyptian presidency then said Saudi and Gulf security is an integral part of Egypt's national security. Saudi Arabia also has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye signed in August, and the three agreed earlier this month to activate deterrence measures and deploy forces to the kingdom.

Analysts told Al Jazeera that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on Red Sea traffic, is an obvious partner. Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging the Houthi attacks, which Tehran rejects. Whether parliament convenes or Riyadh makes a request was not reported.

SpaceX has agreed to buy a large block of low-band spectrum to expand its Starlink network, part of what The Verge describes as a plan to become a major wireless carrier. The Verge's Decoder podcast discussed the deal with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media and telecom.

According to the interview, SpaceX bought 800 MHz of spectrum for $8 billion. That spectrum was originally used by Nextel's push-to-talk service, which Sprint had to divest as part of its sale to T-Mobile, and it was sold to Grain Management before SpaceX bought it. The Verge says SpaceX had already agreed last year to buy close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum. SpaceX says it wants to use the spectrum to build "the world's most advanced mobile network."

Piecyk said satellite companies do not typically pay for spectrum, but SpaceX bought EchoStar spectrum first, received positive investor feedback and then bought more. He described telecom as a trillion-dollar enterprise value business in the US alone. He also said satellites alone are not enough for phones, which have less power and need better coverage indoors, and that the FCC approval of the earlier EchoStar spectrum required a terrestrial component.

The Verge also noted that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-generation Starlink satellites. Its host cautioned that telecom companies often run into how expensive their plans are, and said the industry has a vast graveyard of failed pivots and acquisitions. The podcast explores whether SpaceX can pull this off and how AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile have responded, but the excerpt provided does not include Piecyk's full answers.

According to NPR, President Trump said in early September that he would spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for about 30 Republican candidates in competitive races. At a White House Rose Garden dinner he said, "I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places." NPR reports the White House has not clarified which places he meant, and that Trump has since campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates.

NPR says his travel has instead taken him to Republican territory, including Ohio and Texas twice each, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Arizona, Montana and Alaska. Trump said he visits such states "to thank them" and to support candidates he wants to win. NPR reports he made the eight-hour flight to Alaska to help Sen. Dan Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, whose races it described as close in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

RNC Chairman Joe Gruters told NPR the aim is turnout, saying, "You put the president on the ballot." NPR notes that Trump claims polls showing his approval rating underwater are wrong. It reports he is promoting a $5,000 dividend for every American adult if Republicans win both chambers, an idea that has faced resistance from elected Republicans.

Next, Trump is scheduled to visit Kansas on Monday, where NPR says a Senate race is a toss-up, and Greenville, North Carolina, on Tuesday. NPR reports Republican campaign committees have started canceling ad reservations for Senate candidate Michael Whatley there. North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton said she thinks the visit will backfire on Republicans.

Fox News Digital reports that local organizers of Saturday's "No Kings" demonstrations are using partisan messaging that the national coalition's own rules prohibit. Fox says the day is being turned into a get-out-the-vote effort, and that the coalition did not respond to its request for comment.

According to Fox, event listings in Newark, Delaware, and Roseburg, Oregon, suggested signs such as "Vote Early, Vote Blue" and "Vote them out!" It also cites a Pennsylvania listing that says "Vote Blue." Fox reports that the Placer County Democratic Party in California advertised a canvassing session tied to a rally, even as it described the event as "a day of nonpartisan voter participation."

Fox cites the coalition's host toolkit, which says events must not be partisan or refer to preferred election outcomes, and bars political parties from helping coordinate events. A messaging guide also tells participants not to urge votes for Democrats. Fox says that on a Thursday webinar Indivisible co-founder Ezra Levin told a local group, "By all means, make it about Trump," and said nothing in the No Kings rules prevents focusing on the White House.

Fox says it identified about 300 organizations behind the effort, with estimated annual revenues of $2.5 billion, and about 3,000 events. It describes Indivisible as center-left and says it has received funding from George Soros. It says federal election law bars nonprofits from advocating for particular candidates. Fox's article does not include a response from organizers to its findings.

Final site plans for President Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch do not mention military features he previously said he would add, according to documents the Interior Department submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission, as reported by The Hill. The structure is slated to stand between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

In late September, Trump said the arch would include a "top grade military complex" housing a large number of drones, snipers and ammunition. He said it was added at the military's "strong request." The latest plans do not show those features, but they do include other recent suggestions, such as an eternal flame recommended by the Federal Aviation Administration. The planning commission is set to review the plans at its Nov. 5 meeting.

A White House official, speaking anonymously to The Washington Post, said Trump's plans had not changed and that the administration did not intend to publicly release national security information about the project at this stage. The Post also cited Interior spokesperson Katie Martin, who said the current designs can accommodate national security functions and more. The Hill said it had asked Interior for comment.

The idea drew criticism. Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat whose district includes Arlington, objected to a drone launch site in the landing path for incoming aircraft and said a weapons cache would sit near thousands of pedestrians and commuters. The FAA concluded the arch would not pose a risk to airspace, though Beyer said its review did not consider military drones. John Bolton, Trump's former national security adviser, called the idea "gonzo bonkers."

Rooftop solar installations are surging in the Philippines as electricity prices climb following the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in late February, according to Al Jazeera. Homeowner Keith Cantera said his family's monthly bill rose from about $150 before the war to as much as $220, and that they are now installing panels after years of considering it. He put the cost at up to $5,000, about the same as three or four years of bills at current rates.

The Philippines already had Southeast Asia's highest electricity costs, comparable only to Singapore. The energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the country since early 2025. Chinese government trade data showed $407 million in panel imports from March to May, making the Philippines the biggest single overseas market in that period apart from the Netherlands, which redistributes panels across Europe.

Lexus Grepo, CEO of supplier Solarmaxx, said customers face a 30-day wait because shipments cannot keep up. He said the firm handled 40 projects in March, almost triple its usual monthly clientele, and has since installed 25 to 30 systems a month. He does not expect demand to slow even if Middle East tensions ease.

The country relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power, and the peso has hit a record low of more than 63 to the dollar. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in late March, yet rates have kept rising. Al Jazeera says upfront costs remain too high for most Filipinos, and a government loan program for rooftop systems is open only to public sector workers. Officials point to renewable projects in the pipeline, including a planned large solar farm north of Manila, though some consumers say they could take years.

Scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley report that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active, according to Wired. The findings were published in Nature. Plastic is generally considered chemically stable, and microplastics were thought to share that trait.

The researchers say the activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals that alter other molecules, including ones essential to living organisms, even under normal environmental conditions and without sunlight or other degrading agents. They suggest the difference from larger plastics comes down to surface area. Wei Min, a Columbia professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering, said in a press release that microplastics generate high-energy, reactive radicals in surrounding water that very likely contribute to biological damage seen in animals and potentially humans.

Among the chemicals formed are reactive oxygen species, including hydroxyl radicals, which can take electrons from proteins and fats in cell membranes. The body has antioxidant defenses, but Wired explains they can be overwhelmed, leading to oxidative stress and cell damage. Earlier research had linked microplastic exposure to oxidative stress, though the mechanisms are not fully understood.

In experiments, red blood cells taken from mice became deformed and ruptured when exposed to different microplastics, and the effect was stronger with plastics that reacted more with water. Wired notes that how far microplastics have penetrated human bodies remains debated, and that some of the more sensational findings have been questioned. The researchers argue the results challenge the assumption that microplastics are inert, as the pollutants they carry or release may not be their only hazard.

A 71-year-old man, Steve Hamilton, was killed on Friday by an alligator of almost 12 feet while fishing at a pond in Winter Garden, Florida, according to authorities and media reports cited by The Guardian. WOFL reported, citing local police and the state's fish and wildlife conservation commission, that the animal dragged him into the water from the shoreline.

Emergency crews went to the park at about 5.20pm after a 911 call and tried to rescue him, but WOFL reported that nearby alligators made that difficult. Hamilton's body was recovered from the water a couple of hours later. Capt Michael Mason of the Winter Garden police department said the alligator was killed after the attack.

Mason said authorities had not been alerted to any alligator sighting at the pond on Friday. The pond is connected to Lake Apopka, and he said the water has "tons of alligators in it" and that seeing them in that part of town is not uncommon. He urged people to "be aware of your surroundings," saying the animal "looks like it's docile" but "can be dangerous."

Alligator attacks are statistically rare, The Guardian notes. The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission, which compiles reports of encounters with the state's estimated 1.3 million alligators, says at least 34 people have been killed by them in Florida since 1948. Hamilton's death came less than four months after Brittany Clark, 31, was killed by a 13-foot alligator while swimming in the Econlockhatchee River in Seminole county. Autopsy results released in July showed she struggled for her life before dying.

The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting the Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen cited by The Guardian. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.

The Guardian calls the deal the first tangible sign that a deep UAE-Saudi rift over Yemen's future is starting to heal, because Houthi advances have alarmed the Gulf rulers. Saudi Arabia faces daily drone and missile attacks, and Houthi strikes have immobilised its airports and some of its energy infrastructure. The southern forces, mainly the Giant Brigades, were previously trained and funded by the UAE, which quit operations inside Yemen in January.

Questions remain. Neither country has responded to a demand this week by southern separatists for a referendum on secession. The Southern Transition Council has not agreed to fight outside the old southern borders. Its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed attempt to take charge across the south, and has no direct contact with Saudi officials. The Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try him for treason.

On the ground, Yemen's UN-recognised government declared a counteroffensive last week to drive the Houthis from Sana'a, but it has had limited success near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait. On Friday, two Houthi missiles struck Aden airport about 500 metres from a Yemenia Airways plane, with no casualties reported, according to the information minister. A day earlier, at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.
Egypt's president said he was convening an emergency parliament session to authorise defensive military action for Saudi Arabia. The UN says more than 200,000 people have been displaced.

Several Palestinians were injured by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, and Israeli forces arrested farmers, according to Al Jazeera. The Palestine Red Crescent Society said four women and a child were among six people hurt when settlers attacked residents of Ma'in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron.

Al Jazeera, citing the Palestinian news agency Wafa and its own reporter Nour Odeh, described further incidents. Israeli forces reportedly fired on olive pickers in Deir Ammar, settlers shot and injured two Palestinians nearby, and settlers killed about 20 sheep in Kafr Malek, according to its mayor. Odeh said settlers destroyed olive trees on the Beit Furik plain and fired live ammunition at farmers in Deir Jarir. She cited 300 documented attacks since the start of October. The page text does not include a response from Israeli authorities or settler representatives to these specific reports.

The attacks followed a ruling by Rabbi Dov Lior, who is a spiritual guide for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party. Al Jazeera reports that he wrote that Jews may harvest olives even far from Jewish communities to show ownership of the land, and that Palestinians never bought it. He called the harvesting an additional virtue.

Not all Jewish religious leaders agreed. Rabbis of the Gush Etzion settlements' religious council called taking Palestinian crops theft, and Tzohar, an organisation of 800 Orthodox rabbis, said only the state can confiscate property. Analyst Mamoun Abu Amer suggested political motives could lie behind those rebuttals. Knesset member Gilad Kariv also criticised Lior.
Odeh said politicians allow the violence to continue because it is politically expedient ahead of elections on October 27.

Thousands of Tunisians marched through the capital on Saturday to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms, Al Jazeera reports. The demonstration was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, together with opposition parties and civil society groups.

Al Jazeera described it as the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge him. AFP reported more than 3,000 marchers, though the total could not be independently confirmed. Hundreds of police were deployed and several roads were closed around Habib Bourguiba Avenue.

The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and unemployed people. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to limits on trade union rights. Placards read "No democracy without freedoms" and "No dignity with poverty", and some protesters revived a slogan from the 2011 uprising demanding the government's removal. UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of power in the presidency and said "silence will no longer be acceptable".

Economic complaints ran alongside the political ones. Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, and shortages of medicines and other essentials. One demonstrator from Sfax told Reuters repeated service disruptions had deepened his frustration.

The march followed other protests. In August, demonstrators in Tunis rallied against rising prices, and last month fuel transport workers held a two-day strike over wages and conditions. Saied took power promising an alternative to the post-2011 system. In 2021 he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and deadlock, and a 2022 constitution increased presidential powers. The page text does not include a government response to Saturday's march.

Sudan's army says it killed dozens of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala on Friday, while the RSF says the military killed civilians, Al Jazeera reports. The claims have not been independently confirmed.

In a statement, the army said it targeted RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group's self-declared administration. The RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children. The group has not confirmed or denied that separate army attacks killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres.

The human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market in Nyala was hit on Friday and that the drone used was "affiliated" with the Sudanese army. The army has not been quoted in the page text responding to the market allegation.

Al Jazeera's Almigdad Alruhaid, reporting from Khartoum, said fighting between the army and the RSF has intensified. He cited a Sudanese government source who said the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites in South Kordofan, with exchanges of fire increasing in many parts of the country over the past 24 hours.

The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region with drones in an effort to retake territory held by the RSF, which controls most of the area. This month, army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize "every inch" of RSF-held territory. The war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people, and the United Nations has called the situation the world's worst humanitarian crisis.

Hurricane Trudy held its strength as it moved toward Mexico's western coast on Saturday, and forecasters warned it could strengthen further before weakening on Sunday, Al Jazeera reports. A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco.

The US National Hurricane Center said early Saturday that Trudy was about 305km (190 miles) south-southeast of Manzanillo, with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (90mph), moving at about 13km/h (8mph). It was forecast to approach southwestern and west-central Mexico later Saturday and pass near the coast overnight into Sunday. Hurricane conditions were expected in the warning area on Saturday night, with tropical storm conditions spreading across the region during the day.

Rain is the main concern. The center forecast 10 to 20cm (four to eight inches) across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through the weekend, with isolated totals of about 38cm (15 inches), raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, especially in steep terrain. Outer rain bands could bring two to four inches to Guerrero and Nayarit, where localised flash flooding is possible. The center also warned of possible coastal flooding from storm surge and large, destructive waves.

Swells from Trudy were already affecting parts of the southwestern coast and are expected to spread northward through the weekend, creating life-threatening surf and rip currents. The Mexican navy urged coastal residents and the maritime community to be extremely cautious because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides.
Colima state said its risks are currently low, but significant rainfall could still cause damage because the ground is saturated after successive storms on the Pacific coast.

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey joined a walkout of finance leaders from an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, protesting Russian involvement, The Guardian reports. The group left the session when Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov addressed it in Russian. The Bank of England confirmed Bailey took part.

Bailey was joined by counterparts from France, Germany and several Scandinavian and Baltic countries. Joachim Nagel, president of the German Bundesbank, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure. A European diplomat told Reuters: "The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe. We cannot normalise relations with Russia."

The walkout was acknowledged by Mohammed al-Jadaan, the Saudi finance minister who chairs the IMF's steering committee. He said delegates had come to the meeting for a reason and achieved it, pointing to a chair statement that says all members agreed to it.

The episode shows a split over Russia's place in international bodies. Germany had warned against efforts to bring Russia back onto the international stage, though Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers this year. US treasury undersecretary Erin Browne told Reuters that Washington supported Russia's presence despite European concerns.

On the economy, the meeting heard that the global economy was showing remarkable resilience despite the war between Russia and Ukraine and problems around the strait of Hormuz caused by the US bombing campaign. Al-Jadaan warned against complacency, citing public debt and high bond market rates. His statement said the economy has weathered the latest shocks better than expected, but buffers have been eroded, and that escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt trade routes and worsen energy and food security.

A Chinese nursery owner has been sentenced to life in prison after more than 200 children were poisoned with lead-tainted food, according to Chinese state media cited by the BBC. Li Huifang, who ran the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, Gansu province, was convicted of producing and selling toxic and harmful food.

In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill. A report found chefs had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of meals and attract more students, even though the paint was clearly marked as inedible. Food samples contained lead 2,000 times over China's national safety limit. A red date cake and corn sausage rolls tested at 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg, against a limit of 0.5mg/kg.

The Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered confiscation of 500,000 yuan of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Executive principal Zhi Jinglin received 15 years in prison and a fine of 300,000 yuan. Four kitchen staff were sentenced to between six and eight years; the court found Li and Zhi had instructed them to add toxic ingredients to food served to children and staff.
The World Health Organization says lead poisoning is particularly harmful to young children and can severely damage the brain and central nervous system.

The BBC reports that officials later found dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff had tried to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor. China has since published national guidelines for campus meals, requiring every new batch of food to be tested and flour, rice and cooking oil to be bought only from centralised procurement points.

Americans face significantly higher health insurance costs next month, whether they have Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans or employer coverage, The Hill reports. Some premiums could be the highest in decades, while others will pay more through copays or deductibles, and experts say the pain will become clear when open enrollment begins.

For the roughly 19 million adults on ACA plans, insurers are proposing a median 15 percent premium increase for 2027, according to a KFF analysis of filings in all 50 states and Washington. That is the second straight year of double-digit hikes and the second-highest requested change since 2018. Last year's median finalized increase was 20 percent. Insurers cite rising costs of hospital stays, physician visits and prescriptions, which KFF put at a 10 percent median change, plus expected enrollment declines and a sicker risk pool after enhanced subsidies expired last year when Republicans in Congress let them lapse.

Employer plans are also climbing. A Marsh survey projects costs to rise 8 percent to 10 percent next year, the largest increase in more than 20 years. About 160 million Americans get coverage through work. Last year, family premiums averaged about $27,000, and researchers say workers' out-of-pocket costs can bring their total to around $10,000 for a family. Small businesses may be hit hardest, KFF's Matthew Rae said.

Politics is involved. A KFF poll found healthcare costs, along with gas prices, topped voters' economic concerns in the midterms, and Pew found 64 percent call healthcare very important. The Hill says voters appear to blame Republicans, and Democrats are campaigning on restoring the subsidies. Katherine Hempstead of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation said restoring them would lower what buyers pay but would not address underlying healthcare prices.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed an executive order seeking independent verification of artificial intelligence models and creating an expert committee to examine kill switches for AI agents that could go rogue and cause harm, Al Jazeera reports. It is one of his last executive orders; his final term ends in January.

The order revisits ground from a 2024 bill that Newsom vetoed, saying it would amount to "thwarting the promise of this technology". He now wants to expand the definition of safety incidents and explore a kill switch. He later signed a narrower frontier AI bill in October 2025, which asks large developers to disclose certain safety incidents. Newsom's office told Al Jazeera the vetoed bill was "unworkable" and that no governor has done more on AI risks.

Critics and analysts offered differing readings. Christabel Randolph of the Center for AI and Digital Policy said the order covers only one aspect of the vetoed bill, which she called weaker. Alex Hanna of the Distributed AI Research Institute said Newsom is "setting up his next thing" as he eyes a 2028 presidential run, and doubted the measures would pass during his term. Industry representatives had opposed the 2024 bill, with one venture capitalist calling it a "regressive tax on AI innovation". Syracuse professor Hamid Ekbia argued industry cannot be relied on to regulate itself.

Newsom has asked the California Emergency Services Office for recommendations by November 15 and could convene a special legislative session, possibly before his term ends. Al Jazeera notes this contrasts with the federal government, which has favored industry self-regulation; President Donald Trump last month signed a voluntary accord with several AI leaders.

Many popular websites are blocking AI agents, even as OpenAI, Meta, Google and others promote them as tools that can book dinners, clean out inboxes and buy shoes, The Verge reports. In recent weeks, users of agents including Meta's Muse, xAI's Grok, OpenAI's Dots and Instinct have reported being blocked on top sites.

Yelp told TechCrunch it only allows agents that pay for its data licensing program, and Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets for users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab confirmed they block agents from accessing accounts over security concerns. Some users say Cars.com and Amtrak no longer work, suggesting other companies may be quietly blocking agents.

Amazon has been in a legal fight with Perplexity since last year over its agentic shopping feature. Amazon said third parties buying for customers should respect a site's decision whether to participate. Perplexity argued that Amazon wants human eyes on its ads and does not believe in users' right to have an assistant act for them. A judge ordered Perplexity to stop, an appeals court overturned that in August, and Amazon has filed an amended complaint. Amazon also said Muse's continued access violates its policies, and Elon Musk responded that maybe he "should start a competitor to Amazon".

Meta said turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer, and has partnered with retailers including Walmart, Gap, Sephora and Best Buy. Shopify has opened its storefronts to agents. OpenAI and Google did not immediately comment, and Instinct declined.

Some blocks may come from general anti-bot systems, said Chris Canal of EquiStamp, which also trigger on agents. He warned more verification hurdles could make the web more annoying and reduce the perceived value of AI companies' agents.
